subject: treasureChest
pitch: A pirate's treasure chest with its lid thrown open. Weathered dark wood planks bound with rusty iron straps and studs, a heavy padlock hanging loose, and spilling out of it: gold coins, a pearl necklace, a jewelled goblet and a few red and green gems. A small skull-and-crossbones is carved on the front.
reasoning:
I'm planning the structure of a single TypeScript module using the SDK, sticking to only documented features: boxes for parts, a hinge joint for the lid, studs via stick, and considering whether a decal with an SVG texture could work for a skull design.

Given the uncertainty around the decal and texture APIs, I decide it's safer to build the skull and crossbones from basic primitives like spheres, boxes, and rods shaped with three.js geometry transforms, placing everything with explicit position and orientation rather than relying on ambiguous helper behaviors. For coins, I settle on rotating cylinder geometries directly rather than trusting uncertain direction-based orientation parameters, and I note that parts without an assigned bone will default to the root joint since only the lid needs its own hinge.

I'm now working out the actual coordinates: the chest body is a box centered near the origin sitting on the ground plane, with the lid hinge placed along the back top edge. Since I can't easily rotate a joint after creation to represent the opened lid, I decide to bake the open-lid rotation directly into the lid's geometry before attaching it to the hinge bone, keeping the joint purely for naming rather than runtime posing.

I work out the math for rotating the lid open by about 110 degrees around the hinge axis, calculating how the lid's center point shifts upward and backward from its closed position, then construct the lid box geometry by translating it to the pivot offset, rotating it by that angle, and translating it into place at the hinge location on the chest.

Now I'm planning the chest's contents: a dark interior liner box just below the rim, then piles of treasure spilling over the front edge. I plan coins as small flattened cylinders scattered randomly across the interior with slight tilts in gold tones, gems as small colored polyhedra, pearls as tiny white spheres strung in a necklace shape, and a jeweled goblet built from a lathe-generated cup and stem profile.

For the hardware, I'm adding iron straps and bands across the front, back, and lid with small raised studs, and the body will be built from alternating wood-toned horizontal planks with gaps to suggest wooden boards. I'm also starting on a hanging padlock with a hasp attached to the front clasp.

I'm now figuring out placement for the padlock and a carved skull-and-crossbones motif on the front face, trying to avoid overlap between the hasp, the padlock shackle, and the horizontal strap band, likely offsetting the skull to center and the padlock slightly to one side.

For the skull itself I'm sculpting a bone-colored sphere with dark eye sockets, then building crossbones from two thin cylinders rotated diagonally with small sphere knobs at their ends. I'm also scattering gem octahedrons among the coins and lid interior, and adding spilled coins at floor level around the front rim for visual effect.

I'm now settling on a full color palette—rusty iron, gold, various wood tones, pearl, red, green, and bone white for the skull—plus assuming the rng function returns a callable number generator. I'm structuring the joint hierarchy with a root joint and a lid joint parented to it, then attaching parts via a bone reference and assigning materials by color string.

For positioning, I'm deciding to build each geometry at the origin and bake rotation/translation into the geometry itself before placing it, rather than relying solely on the part's "at" option—working out the transform order (local offset, then rotation, then translation to the pivot) for lid straps and studs so they sit correctly in the closed-lid frame.

I'm now computing the actual numbers for the lid: figuring out the closed-position box dimensions and offsets so the lid sits flush on top of the body, then rotating that position through the open-lid angle to find where the lid's center and extent end up when open, checking the resulting height and depth look geometrically sensible.

Then I'm planning the body construction as a stack of five planks with small gaps filling the 0 to 0.6 height range, sizing each board and gap to land cleanly at the top, and deciding to add iron strap boxes running vertically down the front face to break up the plain wood look.

Now I'm laying out the hardware details: horizontal strap bands across the front at two heights, a decorative skull placed to one side, and a hasp plate positioned centrally to hold a hanging padlock, adjusting positions so nothing overlaps. I'm sketching the padlock itself as a small iron box with a torus shackle on top, placed just below the hasp.

For the coin pile, I'm scattering around 60 small gold cylinders with randomized tilts to fill the chest interior, then adding another 15 coins spilling out over the front edge onto the floor, keeping those flatter and lower to simulate a natural spill.

I'm also planning a draped pearl necklace of 18 small spheres looping through the interior, a goblet shape built from a lathe profile with a cup, base, and stem placed near the coins, and a handful of gem accents (octahedrons in red and green) scattered among the treasure for extra sparkle.

Now I'm figuring out the skull-and-crossbones decoration: a cream sphere for the skull with a scaled jaw box, dark eye sockets, and a nose cone, plus two crossed cylinder "bones" rotated at opposing angles with small end-cap spheres, all positioned near the front face of the body so they appear carved into the surface rather than floating above it.

Then I'm placing decorative studs along the horizontal strap bands, choosing x-coordinates that avoid overlapping with the padlock, hasp, and skull-and-crossbones elements, checking the y-positions so nothing visually collides, and confirming the lid's edge bands and cross straps are consistent with this layout.

I'm adding side vertical straps and corner brackets using small boxes, introducing a two-tone rusty iron palette for variety, and setting up the joint hierarchy with a root "chest" joint and a "lid" joint for the skeleton.

For the geometry, I'm placing the lid parts relative to its own joint pivot so the model-space coordinates stay consistent, then working out the interior cavity's dark box dimensions so its top sits flush with the plank boards without z-fighting.

Now I'm setting up the color palette for wood, iron, brass, gold, pearl, and gem accents, defining the hinge pivot position and open-angle rotation, and starting to scaffold the exported builder function with imports for the 3js builder and seeded RNG utilities.

Still writing chest geometry...

The dark floor just gives the hollow look from the lid's view, with coins stacked on top around 0.62+. For side straps, I'm placing vertical iron bands at x=±0.6 protruding slightly, positioned at a couple z locations on each side, and considering similar placement on front and back.

Adding back straps, front bands, and front vertical straps as iron fixtures, with one band variant in a rusted tone for weathering. I'm thinking about whether to add corner caps but may skip them to keep things simple.

Placing a hasp below the top band, with a padlock body positioned near it and a shackle looping through the hasp opening -- skipping decorative rivets and holes for simplicity.

Working out the padlock's torus-shaped shackle geometry, keyhole detail, and now sketching a skull decoration with a scaled sphere for the skull shape, a jaw box, and eye sockets as small dark spheres.

Adding crossbones as rotated cylinders with sphere knobs at each end, then setting up randomized coin placement inside the chest using position offsets to create a natural mound shape.

Now I'm generating spilled coins scattered outside the chest with varying tilts and positions across the ground and front slope, then starting on a pearl necklace loop computed with trigonometric positions around a center point.

I'm repositioning the necklace to sit on top of the coin pile so it stays visible, then sketching out a lathe-geometry profile for the goblet shape, defining the radius and height points that form its bowl, stem, and base.

I'm placing the goblet into the chest interior with its base resting on the floor, then adding decorative details: red and green gemstones embedded in the cup and a knob on the stem, followed by scattering a handful of octahedron-shaped gems around the scene.

Tallying up the part counts across boards, straps, studs, coins, pearls, gems, goblet, skull, and lid pieces to confirm the total stays comfortably within budget, and checking that nothing floats or clips through the floor. Now I'm working out placement logic for the lid pieces and studs along the front bands, deciding default transforms and positions for each.

Writing lid helper functions...

Placing the hinge geometry at the pivot point without any joint conflicts, then scattering coins randomly across the chest interior with varied heights and slight tilts for a natural pile effect...

I'm adding a spill of flattened coins trailing off the chest edge onto the floor, keeping their bottoms resting at ground level, and arranging pearls in a ring above the coin pile—adjusting coin height ranges so pearls sit visibly on top rather than buried.

I'm scattering gemstone pieces loosely among the coins, then placing a goblet using a lathe-revolved profile for the shape. For the rest, I'm working out precise z-depth placements for the skull decoration, padlock body, keyhole, and hasp so each layered box sits flush against the chest front without clipping.

Now I'm finalizing the skull sphere position and scale, then cleaning up the final code, trimming unused imports, and making sure part options like bone names are correctly attached before writing the complete build.
